newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Traub crisis shows industry woes.
newsitem.headline: German Traub crisis shows industry woes.

text.p: The poor state of Germany's machine tool industry was highlighted on Monday as crisis talks at Traub AG forced a two-day suspension of the cash-strapped toolmaker's shares.
The suspension was requested by Deutsche Bank AG, the leader of a banking pool which was to hold talks with Traub on Monday afternoon on its financial difficulties.
Explaining its decision to remove Traub stock from dealings until Wednesday, the Stuttgart bourse cited "acute developments" at the company and an important announcement expected on Tuesday.
Market rumours were circulating about Traub's trading psoition, but analysts said talk about its ability to survive may be premature.
"Everyone knows that Traub is facing major problems. But to draw any other conclusions would be pure speculation," said Guenther Dielmann of DB Research.

In the red for years and desperately seeking a partner to alleviate its cash problems, Traub has had a disastrous 1996. Its stock has fallen from a year high of 145 marks to a mere 33 marks by the close of trading on Friday.

Hurt by the price pressures hitting the German machine tool industry, Traub's order book dropped 17.1 percent in the first half of 1996, causing its net loss to almost double to 16.4 million marks ($10.71 million).
Last week, the company said it had sold off a substantial chunk of its 50 percent stake in German firm Hermle AG, one of a series of planned measures to shore up its cash position.
Although the group said it was confident of narrowing its full year loss from 16.9 million marks in 1995, Traub revealed last month its banks had refused to sanction plans to seek fresh capital.
That will add urgency to Traub's search for an international partner, the only way to guarantee the firm the capital increase it needs.
German machine tool makers, with the exception of isolated specialist firms, have been under mounting pressure in recent years.

The future of East German machinery toolmaker Sket also hung in the balance this week, as the supervisory board prepared to vote on a radical restructuring to slash the group's workforce to 500 to 1,850.
Deckel Maho AG, one of the leading names in the industry, was rescued from the brink of collapse in mid-1994 when it was taken over by rival company, Gildemeister AG.
Gildemeister has since undergone a broad restructuring. It remains loss-making, although it reduced its net loss in 1995 to 22.9 million marks from 41.1 million marks the previous year.
